The post Mixed messages on higher education: thoughts after the Conservative Party Conference 2026 appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was authored by Charlotte Armstrong, Policy Manager at HEPI.

HEPI’s third and final appearance during this year’s party conference season was at the Conservative Party Conference – you can read our earlier write-ups of what happened at the Reform event here and Labour’s one here. As a non-partisan think tank, we generally try to run events at the annual conferences for both the governing party and the Official Opposition while keeping an eye on, and sometimes attending, some of the others too.

In the run-up to the Conservative event in Birmingham this year, there was lots of talk about the party’s apparent resurgence. Even in Liverpool the week before, there had been discussion as to whether Labour should refocus their attacks on the Tories and leave Reform to their own problems. But despite the build-up, at the Conservative event itself the mood was fairly quiet and the large conference venue was noticeably empty for many of the sessions.

The only protesters in evidence were from Save British Farming, who innovatively made their point from within the secure zone rather than by shouting from the outside. This meant that rather than dodging leaflets and placards, soundtracked by Steve Bray, the only thing I dodged on my approach into Birmingham’s ICC was some secondary school students on a Geography trip trying to survey the police on duty outside the venue.

HEPI’s party conference events generally occur outside the secure zone, to encourage local higher education staff and students not in possession of an expensive conference pass to engage. Our first event was on Soft Power, building on our recent 2026 Soft-Power Index report. We heard from Jamie Arrowsmith (Director of UUK International), Ángel Gurria-Quintana (Director of Stakeholder Relations at Cambridge University Press and Assessment), Professor Duncan Ivison (President and Vice-Chancellor at the University of Manchester) and the former Minister for Universities and Science, the Rt Hon. the Lord Willetts.

The panel provided real balance, with Ángel speaking with pride and passion about his father’s time as a Chevening scholar in Leeds in 1973 and 1974 – he subsequently rose to serve as Secretary of Finance and of Foreign Affairs in Mexico, as well as Secretary-General of the OECD – Ángel noted how his family was a perfect example of the UK’s soft power. It was his father’s experience in the UK that led to Ángel being educated in an English international school, and which influenced his decision to enrol for his postgraduate education in the UK.

In his remarks, Jamie focused in part on the tightening up of the Basic Compliance Assessments and how this was driving a wedge between the Government’s rhetoric on expanding educational exports and the reality on the ground inside institutions. Meanwhile, David Willetts recognised both the soft-power benefits of educating so many people from overseas but also the need for universities to respond to the concerns of local politicians on the pressures on housing in some parts of the country.

Duncan spoke about his experiences growing up in Canada and his time working in senior higher education roles in Australia and made the case that the UK could – but is currently failing to – make the most of the opportunities offered, given key competitor countries are currently making themselves less open to the most ambitious students from around the world.

HEPI’s second event was a Higher Education Question Time, where the speakers, Professor Julie Sanders (Vice-Chancellor and Principal of Royal Holloway), Professor David Mba (Vice-Chancellor of Birmingham City University), Professor Nick Vaughan-Williams (Provost and Vice-Principal of the University of Birmingham) and Baroness Cash (Shadow Minister for Education and Women and Equalities), gamely signed up to be asked anything.

The most striking moment perhaps came from a question from Ruben Persey from the Union of Jewish Students about the rise of antisemitic attacks on campus and what vice-chancellors and others could do to keep their Jewish students safe at a time of heightened tension. The panellists recognised the severity of this issue, the importance of all students feeling like they truly belong to their institutions. The university leaders spoke about the greater levels of engagement they were undertaking with Jewish student groups.

The conversation was also especially animated when the idea of differential fees and the Russell Group’s recent positioning was raised. There was little enthusiasm for the idea of different fees by institutional type from either David Mba or Nick Vaughan-Williams. Even the most objective observer would have been left with the sense that those who want differential fees have more work to do preparing the ground.

Some attendees were pleasantly surprised by the positive messaging from the Shadow Minister, Joanne Cash. She emphasised how keen she is to ensure Baroness Smith, the Minister for Skills, receives appropriate parliamentary scrutiny across the despatch box in the House of Lords. As well as noting the vital and broad economic and societal contributions made by higher education institutions, Baroness Cash was less relaxed than some Conservative voices have sometimes sounded on the risk of university closures.

Across the Conservative Conference as a whole, there weren’t as many events on higher education as there had been in Liverpool the previous week but, after getting lost multiple times, I managed to find my way to a backroom at the farthest reaches of the venue to speak at a More in Common/UCL Policy Institute event. Entitled ‘Shared Institutions: the role of universities in local and national life’, it began with More in Common presenting some interesting data on public attitudes towards higher education and universities. It offered a nice change of pace for a sector that has recently been under fire from media and politicians alike: when compared to other institutions, universities are thought of remarkably well.

The public, we were told, is not particularly concerned about free-speech debates on campus, and negative perceptions of higher education institutions tend to be more strongly associated with employment outcomes than with culture wars. Interestingly, while the research role of institutions was described as a topic that ‘rarely came up unprompted’ in focus groups with the general public, it is also one of the areas where people feel most positive towards and about higher education institutions. Perhaps there is something for the sector to consider in the future, not least as part of Universities UK’s current work on how the sector is perceived.

Rebecca Smith MP, who has recently joined Laura Trott and Saqib Bhatti on the Shadow Education team, urged higher education institutions to publicise their civic engagement better, though some present felt their existing contribution (and the efforts they go to promote it) was perhaps already greater than parliamentarians tend to recognise.

I spoke at the event about the importance of listening and reaching out to communities as part of universities’ civic engagement work. The More in Common polling shows non-graduates are less likely than graduates to say that universities have a positive impact on the country and on local areas (although over 50 per cent say they do on both counts). Universities shouldn’t be telling people that they’re wrong for thinking that – non-graduates are forming their opinions based on their own lived experience. Instead, they need to reach out to cold spots and communities where fewer people have historically gone on to higher education to ensure that they feel the benefits of these institutions, even if residents never actually step through the doors and sit in their lecture halls. The UPP Foundation has done some really interesting work using the case study of Doncaster to explore this issue.

As I sat on the train back from Birmingham, I was grateful for the engagement we had seen with HEPI’s work but was also left with the sense that the Conservative Party is sending somewhat mixed messages about our sector. Real recognition of the contribution universities make was on show in Birmingham, a city rammed full of higher education institutions with different missions, but quickfire attacks on both institutions and international students were present in view, and the party apparently remains committed to big cuts in the number of student places. If the Conservative Party moves closer to power in the future, that tension will need to be resolved if we are to understand what the Party really think of higher education.

full_text:
Procrastination is the biggest problem that can harm students’ academic performance at university, according to a study of more than 65,000 young people who placed it above issues such as ADHD, anxiety or financial worries.

The study found that nearly half of the students surveyed named procrastination as the thing damaging their ability to do academic work, more than twice the number who named depression, while the same proportion said procrastination caused them significant distress above any other problems including family pressures or bullying.

Itamar Shatz, the author of the study and an affiliated lecturer at the University of Cambridge, said that while he expected the survey of US students would show that they experienced harm from procrastination, he was surprised by how strongly it affected them.

Shatz said: “Pretty much all of us procrastinate but it’s not a huge impediment for all of us. For the people that it is, it can be huge. It’s not just something we occasionally run into but, as we can see in these findings, it can be a major obstacle.

“It’s an obstacle that can interfere with academic success, with success in the workplace, it can cause issues in relationships, it can cause stress, it can cause health issues and stop us reaching out for help.”

The study, published in the journal Plos One, also suggests that procrastination could be a factor in a “vicious cycle” that can cause or exaggerate other issues such as stress.

“An example of such a feedback loop is a student procrastinating on a task, which causes them to feel stressed, which interferes with their sleep, which causes them to procrastinate on the task further,” the study said.

Fuschia Sirois, a psychology professor at Durham University and a co-editor-in-chief of the British Journal of Health Psychology, who was not involved in the study, said: “The salience of procrastination in students’ lives and its harms has been a topic of research for almost 30 years, with the first studies on the impact of procrastination on health and wellbeing conducted in the late 1990s and early 2000s. So this is an issue for which there is an established evidence base that clearly highlights the negative impact of procrastination on students’ lives.

“This descriptive study with a large sample provides some additional insights into the relative impact of procrastination with respect to its range of harms. But it is just a snapshot, so limits the conclusions we can draw.”

Sirois said myths about procrastination “being a character flaw” have persisted despite the existing research.

“People procrastinate to avoid the difficult emotions associated with a task, which affords them short-term mood repair. But in the long run the feelings of guilt, shame and stress from procrastinating catch up to them and take a toll on health and wellbeing,” she said.

Shatz, who has recently published a guide to overcoming procrastination, said that procrastination should not be compared with laziness, because procrastinators can often be highly motivated to tackle a task only to be derailed by other distractions such as perfectionism or burn-out.

Universities should be aware that many of their students are likely to be hampered by procrastination.

“They should understand that procrastination isn’t just a time management flaw that they can fix with a flyer, but it is one of the biggest obstacles that students face and needs to be treated with positive interventions. The good thing is that research shows that interventions can help,” Shatz said.

title: Lincoln U Students, Alumni Sue Missouri for $549M, Citing Underfunding
summary:
Lincoln U Students, Alumni Sue Missouri for $549M, Citing Underfunding
Olivia.sanchez Wed, 10/07/2026 - 06:22 PM

Lawyers for the 1890 Project said the group plans to legislate, litigate or negotiate for repayment from all 16 states with a documented history of underfunding historically Black land-grant universities.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
A group of current and former Lincoln University students filed a federal lawsuit Wednesday against the state of Missouri, seeking $548.7 million owed to the Black land-grant institution for funds the state neglected to allocate to the university between 1987 and 2020, plus interest.

The filing marks the beginning of a campaign by a group called the 1890 Project to seek repayment of the $12.6 billion of documented underfunding of historically Black land-grant colleges in 16 states. Donald Calloway Jr., the group’s lead attorney, said they will pursue repayment through litigation, negotiation and legislation.

The lawsuit argues that seven current and former Lincoln University students suffered personal and professional damages as a result of the chronic underfunding. The plaintiffs said they experienced inadequate infrastructure in dorms and academic buildings, limited hours at a dining hall that provided mostly unhealthy food, and insufficient student support services.

If Lincoln had received fair funding between 1987 and 2020, as mandated by federal law, the money would have gone toward better facilities and more opportunities, Calloway said.

The lawsuit alleges that the state violated the students’ 14th Amendment rights by failing to enforce both the 1890 law, which requires states to equitably fund historically Black-land grant colleges and the existing land-grant institutions that then only allowed white students, and their violated civil rights by discriminating based on race. The current and former students are asking for the $548.7 million to be paid back with federal supervision, as well as a plan to ensure equal funding for Lincoln University in the future.

“The reality is, the harm inflicted upon Lincoln or Southern or each one of these individual [institutions] is, when you look at it at scale, indicative of harm inflicted over Black America,” Calloway said. “[The underfunding] has affected the lives of generations of African Americans throughout the South.”

The lawsuit names the state of Missouri; Gov. Mike Kehoe; the state higher education coordinating board; Bennett Boggs, commissioner of higher education; and Mun Y. Choi, the president of the University of Missouri system, the state’s 1862—that is, predominantly white—land-grant institution. Through a spokesperson, Kehoe declined to comment on the pending litigation.

Momentum toward the lawsuit has been building for years. In 2023, the Biden administration wrote to the governors of 16 of the 19 states with historically Black land-grant institutions to highlight the value of the institutions, calling for the repayment of the funds—calculated on a per-student basis—over time. The letter to Missouri’s then-governor, Mike Parson, said the state had underfunded Lincoln University by more than $361 million over three decades.

“These funds could have supported infrastructure and student services and would have better positioned the university to compete for research grants,” the administration wrote. “Lincoln University has been able to make remarkable strides and would be much stronger and better positioned to serve its students, your state, and the nation if made whole with respect to this funding gap.”

The letters to all 16 states were previously available on the federal Education Department website but appear to have been removed at some point in the past six weeks. ED did not respond to a request to clarify whether the letters had been relocated to a different site or removed altogether. (Inside Higher Ed was able to find them on the Wayback Machine.)

Burst Pipes, Salty Food

In the lawsuit, Makhi Joseph Berinyuy Jaff, a plaintiff who attended Lincoln in 2023 and 2024, said he was assigned to a residence hall built in 1963, where he at times experienced cold water and faulty water pressure in the restrooms. He also reported that while living in the dorm, a pipe burst and “caused fecal matter to disperse throughout the building.” Across campus, he alleged, students experienced Wi-Fi outages, exposed pipes and broken brick walls. In the dining hall, he said, students were served undercooked meat as well as food with low nutritional value and high sodium content. He left Lincoln without a degree and is currently working for an hourly wage of $15, according to the lawsuit.

Jaydan Monee Ware, a current sophomore who serves as the student body treasurer, said in the lawsuit that she lost 15 pounds during her freshman year because the dining hall closed before her band practice ended.

“There’s a broad universe of demonstrable harm that affects the current students’ experience on campus,” Calloway said. And it extends to “alumni who are still competing in the workplace with a devalued degree, who have diminished earning power as a result of that devalued degree.”

Another plaintiff, Herbert J. Kitchen, is a great-great-grandson of one of the formerly enslaved soldiers who founded the university as the Lincoln Institute in 1866. As a Lincoln student in the 1980s, Kitchen said, outdated infrastructure in the dorms distracted him from his schoolwork and caused stress. He told Inside Higher Ed that the buildings’ heat only worked sometimes, and the water heater regularly gave out in the winter, meaning that he and the other students had to boil water in their dorm mother’s kitchen to wash their faces at night.

Kitchen said the university went through a number of presidents during his time there, which led to overall instability. He graduated from Lincoln in 1988 with a bachelor’s degree in marketing and went on to spend most of his career as a community college administrator in California. Still, he believes his degree doesn’t carry as much weight as it might have if Lincoln had been funded appropriately.

“The state of Missouri thought of Lincoln University as a stepchild,” Kitchen said. “Had the state of Missouri put Lincoln on the same playing field as the other schools, I believe Lincoln would have prospered.”

Calloway, the attorney, was elected to the Missouri House of Representatives in 2009 and served one term—which took place during the identified period of Lincoln’s underfunding, from 1987 to 2020, according to the lawsuit. That means he was part of the State Legislature that failed to fund Lincoln equitably. He noted the irony of his current fight against the state for those funds, but said his experience as a lawmaker gives him some insight into how the underfunding went on for so long.

“I think a lot of the legislators, as well as attorneys general and governors and commissioners of higher education, have just accepted the funding mechanisms and the funding scheme that they were given without really questioning it,” Calloway said. “You just kind of rubber-stamp and pass it along. Very few people take the opportunity to examine why things are set up as they are. Even if they do examine it and realize there’s some fundamental unfairness there, a lot of folks don’t want to upset the apple cart for a variety of reasons.”

title: University of Arizona Temporarily Suspends All Fraternity Activities
summary:
University of Arizona Temporarily Suspends All Fraternity Activities
jessica.blake@… Wed, 10/07/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
The University of Arizona put an interim pause on activities for all 21 of its fraternities Monday amid a series of ongoing misconduct investigations, according to a letter the university shared with Inside Higher Ed.

In the letter, Dean of Students Chrissy Lieberman wrote that seven weeks into the semester, the university is “already” investigating nearly half of its fraternities for incidents including physical assault, hazing and inappropriate use of drugs and alcohol.

“The number of cases under investigation and the severity of the concerns is egregious,” Lieberman wrote to the “Arizona Fraternity and Sorority Community.” She noted that UA President Suresh Garimella met with the fraternity presidents over the summer, calling their chapters’ behavior “unacceptable” and warning that the university “will not tolerate further violations that put our students in harm’s way.”

Arizona’s decision to crack down on its Greek life system comes in the midst of a nationwide conversation over sexual misconduct at fraternities following a lawsuit against Cornell University for allegedly mishandling a 2024 allegation of gang rape at Chi Phi.

UA's fraternity chapters are temporarily barred from hosting, sponsoring or participating in any organizational activities until the chapter advisers meet with Lieberman, her letter said. If they attend at least one of the three scheduled mandatory meetings and are in good standing, they will be allowed to resume activity. Quarterly follow-up meetings will also be required.

“As you know, the value of the Greek experience is under scrutiny nationwide,” she wrote. “It is time for the University of Arizona Greek community to step up and set an example for good. It is time to have difficult conversations with each other and the members of the community.”

title: Helping Stopped-Out Students Finish College
summary:
Helping Stopped-Out Students Finish College
Joshua.Bay Wed, 10/07/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new University of Houston–Downtown initiative pairs re-enrollment efforts with financial and basic needs support while examining institutional barriers to completion.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Colleges nationwide go to great lengths to re-enroll the millions of Americans who have left higher education with credits but no credential. But bringing students back doesn’t necessarily address the financial, academic and personal challenges that led them to leave in the first place.

A new two-year initiative at the University of Houston–Downtown is testing a more comprehensive approach: It combines personalized advising with emergency financial assistance, community-based basic needs support and efforts to change institutional policies that can make returning to college difficult for working adults.

Backed by $975,000 in philanthropic support, Bridge to Completion aims to create a centralized re-engagement hub for former students who have stopped out since 2018. There, students can receive individualized outreach, degree mapping, academic advising, assistance with readmission and financial aid, career guidance, and personalized plans for returning to college.

Jonathan Davis, interim senior vice president for academic affairs and provost, said the university developed the initiative with the understanding that the stopped-out student population can face an array of challenges as they restart their academic careers. Those can include unpaid institutional balances, transportation and childcare costs, and unexpected expenses.

“Every student’s story is their own, and everyone is a little different, but they kind of rhyme in ways that you notice over time,” Davis said. “By having a coherent effort around these specific populations of high need and high opportunity, then we know we can deploy those resources.”

Removing barriers to return: The initiative will also examine institutional barriers working adults are often up against, including scheduling and prior-learning policies, as well as access to online and flexible course options and opportunities for competency-based education.

“When we write policies, we’re never looking to create barriers, but those barriers can sometimes creep in,” Davis said. “This effort is a statement of purpose and a statement of willingness of the institution to re-examine those policies.”

Davis said the initiative responds to a significant challenge facing both UHD and Texas: Thousands of people have earned college credits but left higher education without receiving a credential.

“It’s a significant population,” Davis said. “And for a university like ours serving a population of students that’s predominantly first generation and economically disadvantaged … it often relates to family obligations and financial distress.”

Roughly 70 percent of UHD’s nearly 14,000 students are first generation—a significantly higher share than the national average of 54 percent and Texas average of 43.5 percent.

The initiative comes as institutions and states nationwide have prioritized reaching this population as a way to increase educational attainment and boost enrollment. Michigan, for example, has partnered with ReUp Education to reconnect these learners with higher education as part of the state’s goal to have 60 percent of working-age adults earn a postsecondary credential by 2030.

UHD expects to reach more than 2,000 former students, support approximately 600 through readmission and help at least 500 re-enroll. The university is targeting a persistence rate of approximately 70 percent among returning students and plans to document which strategies are most effective for different student populations.

The initiative is backed financially by the Greater Texas Foundation, the William Stamps Farish Fund and the Alliance of Community Assistance Ministries. Funding will support the university’s re-engagement infrastructure as well as provide direct assistance for students facing financial barriers. Through its partnership with the Alliance of Community Assistance Ministries, UHD will also connect returning students with community-based aid for food, housing, utilities and other basic needs.

Such help is vital; an analysis from the Hope Center for Student Basic Needs at Temple University found that despite growth in emergency aid programs on college campuses, far fewer students are receiving that assistance. Drawing on data from Trellis Strategies’ most recent Student Financial Wellness Survey, the analysis found that the share of students receiving emergency aid fell from 44 percent in fall 2021 to 4 percent in fall 2025.

The Trellis survey also found that more than half of respondents experienced at least one form of basic needs insecurity. Over half (54 percent) said they would struggle to access $500 in cash or credit for an unexpected expense, while 65 percent said they had run out of money at least once since the start of the year.

“There’s not necessarily attention paid to the fact that they have barriers in place to begin with that cause them to step away,” Davis said. “What’s exciting about this is that it’s an opportunity for us to put together a care team on the front end proactively to understand that the student who is returning is someone who’s coming with those challenges to begin with.”

Defining success: Davis said the ultimate measure of the initiative’s success will be whether returning students graduate, advance in their careers and improve their families’ economic circumstances.

“All of the numbers are waypoints along the way,” Davis said. “The 2,000 [former] students and 600 through readmission and 500 re-enrolled—that’s all great, but those are just markers in my head to ‘How do we get students through to the finish line and add to their lives and to the Texas economy?’”

title: BSC Education enters liquidation, ceases trading
summary:
The English language school group with centres in the UK, Malta is entering liquidation.

The post BSC Education enters liquidation, ceases trading appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
“It is with great sadness that we announce that BSC Education Ltd will cease trading and enter liquidation,” the company said in a statement.

The group did not disclose details of the liquidation or the reasons behind it, but told partners that its “immediate priority is supporting our current students providing information to those with future bookings”.

During what it describes as “an extremely difficult time for everyone connected with BSC Education” the company said it is “working closely with English UK and other stakeholders to help students continue their studies through alternative accredited schools” and added that students, agents and partners are being contacted directly with further information about their individual circumstances.

BSC Education is an international English language school group with accredited centres in the UK and Malta, as well as an online school. Its schools host adult students, young learners, and teachers from around the world. [A separate legal entity operates in Kuwait]

“BSC Education has welcomed thousands of students from around the world, providing educational opportunities, cultural experiences and pathways to personal and professional growth,” the statement continued.

“We are immensely proud of the impact our schools, staff and partners have made and of the global community that has been built over the years.”

“We would like to thank our students, agents, educational partners, accommodation hosts and suppliers. Above all, we thank our dedicated staff, past and present, for their trust, support and commitment. Their contribution has been central to everything BSC Education has achieved.”

The news comes at a difficult time for the English language sector, following EC English Language Centres’ confirmation that it is closing all 25 of its language schools across seven destinations with immediate effect.

title: Trump administration proposes $70,000 OPT fee
summary:
The Trump administration has proposed charging US universities $70,000 for each international student they recommend for Optional Practical Training (OPT), with institutions facing further annual fees for extensions.

The post Trump administration proposes $70,000 OPT fee appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the proposed rule on October 7, under which institutions would pay an additional $30,000 per year for extensions of a student’s initial OPT.

In its current form, OPT offers international students on F-1 visas an opportunity to gain work experience in their field of study for 12 months after graduation, while remaining in student status. Eligible STEM graduates can extend the program for a further two years.

The program is central to America’s appeal as a study destination, and its growing popularity has been a driving force behind rising international student numbers in recent years.

NAFSA CEO Fanta Aw said the proposed fee structure was the latest development creating “deep uncertainty” for international students.

“OPT enables international students to gain the same hands-on experience as their domestic peers while filling labor shortages in high-demand STEM fields and generating jobs for US workers on US soil,” she continued.

Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership

Fanta Aw, NAFSA

“The research is clear: international students don’t take opportunities from Americans, they create them. Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership.”

NAFSA said it would mobilise its members to submit detailed comments on the proposed rule.

title: Russell Group universities to showcase UK higher ed at China open days
summary:
Fifteen UK research-intensive universities will take part in collaborative events in Shanghai and Beijing designed to highlight future skills, academic excellence and the long-term value of a UK education.

The post Russell Group universities to showcase UK higher ed at China open days appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Fifteen of the twenty-four Russell Group universities will come together in China this month for two open day events aimed at promoting UK higher education and giving prospective students and their families a deeper insight into the UK study experience.

The events, co-created and delivered by the China-Britain Business Council (CBBC), will be held on October 24 at The Langham, Shanghai, and October 25 at CP Grand Hall in Beijing.

Participating universities are: Newcastle University, University of Sheffield, University of Glasgow, Nottingham University, University of Liverpool, University of Warwick, University of Exeter, University of Birmingham, Cardiff University, Durham University, University of Leeds, Queen Mary University, Queen’s University Belfast, University of Southampton and University of York.

The Russell Group open days will focus on ‘future skills’ and look to encourage students to consider how a research-intensive UK education can help prepare them for the global workforce.

Academic pavilions themed around AI, digital innovation and green futures will showcase university research and invite students to explore the knowledge and capabilities needed for emerging careers, a spokesperson for CBBC told The PIE.

Catherine Shipley, senior advisor for education at CBBC UK HQ, said the upcoming program “responds to sector demand for a more collaborative approach to student recruitment and to student feedback about making university engagement feel less transactional”.

“We want parents and students to have meaningful engagement with academics, alumni and employers from a range of institutions, and for the experience to be enjoyable and memorable,” she added.

We also want to give families the opportunity to understand UK universities and UK education beyond rankings, by making the experience more personal and accessible

Catherine Shipley, CBBC UK HQ

“We also want to give families the opportunity to understand UK universities and UK education beyond rankings, by making the experience more personal and accessible,” said Shipley.

Designed as a collaborative higher education showcase rather than a traditional recruitment fair, the open days will “bring together academic and recruitment colleagues, alumni, employers and sponsors from the 15 participating universities”, according to CBBC.

Content will highlight employability, graduate outcomes, career readiness and the long-term value of a UK education, alongside the global research standing of Russell Group universities and their contribution to social and economic development.

title: Spotlight on… Te Herenga Waka, Victoria University of Wellington
summary:
The PIE sat down with Victoria University of Wellington to discuss the future of international education, New Zealand’s growing global appeal and what sets studying in the country’s capital apart.

The post Spotlight on… Te Herenga Waka, Victoria University of Wellington appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
1. Tell us about your university and its role within New Zealand’s higher education landscape.

Te Herenga Waka—Victoria University of Wellington is New Zealand’s globally ranked capital city university, located in the heart of Wellington, the country’s political, cultural, and innovation centre. With a strong reputation for research, teaching excellence, and public engagement, we play an important role in connecting students with government, industry, and community partners. We rank in the top 100 universities in the world for AI, English Language and Literature, Library and Information Management, Linguistics, and Law (QS Rankings, Shanghai Rankings, 2026). As New Zealand’s top-ranked university for research intensity (PBRF, 2018), we are committed to developing graduates who can help address local, national, and global challenges while advancing knowledge that delivers real-world impact.

2. What sets your university apart from others?

Our location is one of our greatest strengths. Being based in New Zealand’s capital city gives our students unparalleled access to decision-makers, government agencies, international organisations, creative industries, and leading employers. We combine world-class academic performance with a highly connected, real-world learning environment. Students benefit from strong industry engagement, research-led teaching, and opportunities to build practical skills and professional networks while studying in one of the world’s most liveable cities.

3. What makes New Zealand such an attractive destination for international students?

New Zealand offers an exceptional combination of academic quality, safety, lifestyle, and career opportunities. Students choose New Zealand because they can receive a globally respected education in a welcoming, multicultural society while enjoying an outstanding quality of life. The country is known for its natural beauty, innovative outlook, and strong focus on student wellbeing. International students also value the opportunity to gain practical experience, develop global career skills, and study in an environment that encourages independent thinking and creativity.

Being based in New Zealand’s capital city gives our students unparalleled access to decision-makers, government agencies, international organisations, creative industries, and leading employers

4. How do you see the higher education sector in New Zealand evolving over the next five years?

We expect New Zealand’s higher education sector to become increasingly focused on international engagement, innovation, and student outcomes. Universities will continue strengthening partnerships with industry, expanding flexible learning opportunities, and responding to global workforce needs. There will also be greater emphasis on employability, transnational education, and delivering a more connected student experience. New Zealand is well positioned to grow its international education sector through its reputation for quality, safety, and authentic student experiences, while remaining competitive in a rapidly changing global market.

5. Are there particular markets or student segments you’re looking to grow in the near future?

Alongside maintaining strong relationships in established markets, particularly in Asia, we are focused on broadening our international student population and growing enrolments in areas where there is strong alignment between student demand and our academic strengths. We are also increasingly interested in students seeking career-focused experiences, postgraduate qualifications, and opportunities that combine academic study with employability outcomes, leadership development, and global citizenship skills.

Spending time exploring New Zealand’s beautiful natural environment. Whether it’s walking along a rugged coastline, hiking through native forests, or experiencing our national parks, New Zealand offers a sense of space and connection to nature that is difficult to find elsewhere. Visitors often arrive for the scenery, but they leave remembering the warmth of the people and the uniquely relaxed, outdoors-focused lifestyle that makes New Zealand so special.

title: CU Denver takes step towards India campus in Hyderabad
summary:
The university says it is the first public US institution authorised to establish a degree-granting campus in India, with an August 2027 intake planned.

The post CU Denver takes step towards India campus in Hyderabad appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The University of Colorado Denver has received a letter of intent from India’s University Grants Commission (UGC) to establish a campus in Hyderabad, where it plans to welcome its first students in August 2027.

CU Denver says the decision makes it the first public American university authorised to establish a degree-granting location in India and the first foreign university to receive a letter of intent for a campus in Telangana. The university must still complete further regulatory processes before opening.

The proposed campus will offer study pathways in business, computing, engineering and analytics, combining academic teaching with practical experience and interdisciplinary learning. Additional programs will be submitted to the UGC for approval from the second year onwards.

Global education company Emeritus will act as CU Denver’s strategic joint venture partner, supporting the campus’s establishment and growth through non-academic functions.

The announcement did not specify individual degree titles, tuition fees or an enrolment target. Students are expected to remain connected to the university’s US home campus, although the announcement did not outline any mobility arrangements.

“Expanding access to high-quality education has long been central to CU Denver’s vision and goals,” said chancellor Kenneth T. Christensen.

“Our plans in Hyderabad build on that commitment, as well as our longstanding connection with students from India who have been part of the CU Denver community for decades.”

The initiative will create opportunities for students and provide greater access to an education that is both academically rigorous and closely connected to the world of work

Ashwin Damera, Emeritus

The university’s plans follow Illinois Institute of Technology’s Mumbai expansion. Illinois Tech became the first US university authorised to establish a degree-granting campus in India, receiving a UGC letter of intent in 2025 followed by a letter of approval in 2026.

Employer involvement is central to Illinois Tech’s approach. As previously reported by The PIE News, its Mumbai model includes industry input into curriculum and teaching, alongside paid placements integrated into degrees.

For Emeritus co-founder and CEO Ashwin Damera, the proposed CU Denver campus similarly responds to demand for education with a strong connection to employment.

“The proposed University of Colorado Denver | Hyderabad marks an important step in bringing globally relevant education closer to students in India,” he said.

“CU Denver’s focus on applied learning, interdisciplinary education, and career readiness is particularly relevant to the aspirations of today’s students and the needs of a rapidly evolving workforce. The initiative will create opportunities for students and provide greater access to an education that is both academically rigorous and closely connected to the world of work.”

The Hyderabad announcement also comes as Telangana seeks to attract overseas institutions as part of its ambition to develop a ‘Global Knowledge Hub’.

Chief minister A Revanth Reddy said in September that the University of London and Northeastern University planned to establish offshore campuses in Hyderabad, as per reports.

The University of Birmingham has reportedly expressed interest in Telangana’s planned “Future City” development, as the state’s chief secretary has directed officials to prepare a policy covering infrastructure, investment and approvals for international campuses.

As CU Denver develops its own campus with academic and industry stakeholders, Christensen said the university hoped to extend the experience it already offers Indian students in the US.

“We now have an opportunity to extend that connection and bring our unique experience to students in India—combining rigorous academics, career-aligned learning, and real-world experience that prepare students for meaningful careers and contributions to their communities.”

title: What IT Leaders Need To Know Before Deploying a Campus Mental Health Platform
summary:
The concept of universities offering mental health resources to students isn’t new, but 24/7 online mental health platforms are gaining traction with higher education institutions. With these platforms, students can access remote resources whenever they need assistance. However, these tools introduce a challenge for IT leaders: the management of protected health information. 
As institutions increasingly adopt these tools, the overall review process for new technology typically remains the same. The mental health component, however, means institutions should be leveraging the knowledge…
full_text:
Standard Technology Review Practices Apply

Regardless of the technology and intent, the procurement and security review processes are fairly similar, explains Zach Rossmiller, associate vice president and CIO at the University of Montana. Rossmiller describes the University of Montana’s technology review process as rigorous and demanding, ensuring compliance with federal and state laws, accessibility standards, and cybersecurity checks. The university also asks for a SOC 2 report and uses the Higher Education Community Vendor Assessment Toolkit.

The HECVAT template is the product of combined efforts of EDUCAUSE, Internet2 and REN-ISAC. It’s used by higher education to get a “detailed picture” of a prospective vendor’s “cybersecurity, privacy, IT accessibility and compliance standards in one place,” according to EDUCAUSE.

Lipscomb University relies on HECVAT as well, says Brett Hinson, vice president of IT and CIO. “The report allows us to thoroughly evaluate a vendor’s security posture, data encryption and access controls tailored specifically to our campus environment,” he says.

In addition to this process for any proposed technology, mental health platforms introduce access or integration with protected health information and personally identifiable information, which means more laws — such as HIPAA — are in play.

WATCH: In this webinar, CDW experts discuss how to manage third-party risk.

“Every university looking at these tools should have a vendor risk management program,” Rossmiller says. “They should have strong data governance and a HIPAA compliance officer, CISO and CIO who are a pyramid of experts, actively reviewing and pushing back on the vendors to ensure that they’re protecting their student data.”

Collaborating Across the University for the Protection of Students

When it comes to a mental health platform, Rossmiller encourages IT leadership to also consider the expertise of their faculty and staff. While IT handles the integration requirements, data access controls and cybersecurity, these mental health experts — whether faculty or counselors — can assess how the platform interacts with students and vice versa to ensure a safe environment, especially during critical moments.

Lipscomb University’s partnership with TimelyCare, a virtual health provider, began during the COVID-19 pandemic when the university was searching for an alternative to on-campus resources, explains Kevin Eidson, director of health and wellness at Lipscomb.

“What began as a response to an immediate crisis has become an important part of our ongoing commitment to supporting the emotional and physical well-being of every student in the Lipscomb community,” he says.

DISCOVER: Artificial intelligence is supporting mental health initiatives.

Eidson also says that cross-departmental collaboration at the university is imperative for the success of a mental health platform and for the safety and benefit of students.

“While IT professionals provide critical expertise related to technology, cybersecurity, privacy and system integration, faculty, counselors, healthcare providers and student life professionals bring an important understanding of students’ needs and how the service will function within the broader campus support system,” he says.

Hinson says it’s this very group, the folks outside of IT, who are the day-to-day overseers of the platform. Once IT has reviewed and approved the vendor — barring any unexpected changes to terms and conditions or offerings— and enabled the necessary integration requirements, the ownership transitions.

“Faculty and staff must understand its value and support the partnership,” says Eidson. “They are often the people students trust and turn to first, so their willingness to promote the service, explain how it can help, and refer students to it is a vital part of increasing awareness and utilization.”

READ MORE: Higher ed IT leaders are rethinking vendor risk.

Considerations for Implementation and Deployment

As with any other platform or tool, the same steps and conversations should be had with a mental health vendor with regard to access and retention of student data, says Rossmiller.

He advises:

Data retention is a major concern. If a vendor uses a chatbot feature, for example, universities must understand how the student interactions and student data are being used to train their artificial intelligence (AI) — and put a stop to it as needed.

Ask for references that reflect the region and size of your institution. Rossmiller also asks for references of former clients — though he rarely receives them. He wants a clear picture of the positives and negatives with a comparable institution, and information about how they handled the deployment.

Gone are the days when contracts were reviewed once per fiscal year. With new features and AI enablement, IT teams are left constantly scrambling to pause tech and reassess the risk and legal concerns. Look for a vendor who is willing to be a partner and not adjust terms and conditions without warning. These kinds of vendors can also help tell the story of how your university is using the tool for the betterment and benefit of students.

Rossmiller says that he cannot have a conversation without AI being brought up, and the discussion about mental health tech deployment is no different. His concern stems from students potentially turning to AI chatbots as a substitute for a human professional in a vulnerable moment. It’s scenarios like this that highlight the value and importance of relying on university mental health faculty and staff to assess every aspect of a potential new mental health tool before it’s shared with students.

“Broad institutional involvement helps ensure that the service is safe, clinically appropriate, responsive to students’ needs and effectively integrated into the university’s overall approach to student well-being,” says Eidson.

title: Tell it slant: what universities miss in the joins
summary: by Joanne Irving-Walton Universities are increasingly good at recording fragments of student experience. But fragments do not automatically make a whole. The work of connecting them remains stubbornly human. “Tell all the truth but tell it slant —” Emily Dickinson … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Joanne Irving-Walton

Universities are increasingly good at recording fragments of student experience. But fragments do not automatically make a whole. The work of connecting them remains stubbornly human.

“Tell all the truth but tell it slant —” Emily Dickinson advises.

It is an odd instruction for universities increasingly committed to straight lines: lines of accountability, lines between strategy and delivery, pathways through programmes, and data intended to show, cleanly and conclusively, what is happening. Yet neither learning nor universities behave quite like this. Students move between modules, systems, academic staff, professional services, regulations, placements and increasingly distributed forms of provision. Each part of the institution sees something. None necessarily sees the whole.

At the same time, we are becoming increasingly accomplished at recording these fragments. Attendance is captured. VLE activity can be traced. Marks, referrals, extensions and interventions leave institutional records. Processes generate evidence that something has happened. Reliable systems, fair regulations, consistent decisions and clear routes to support all matter. The problem begins when increasingly detailed representations of student experience are mistaken for increasingly complete understanding of it. A university can know a great deal about what a student has done while understanding remarkably little about what is happening.

Students experience the joins

Students rarely experience universities as organisational charts. They encounter them at the joins: between module and course, academic and pastoral support, partner and university, attendance and wellbeing, policy and circumstance, one team’s responsibility and another’s. This is where seemingly small difficulties can accumulate.

A student is sent the correct information but does not understand what they need to do next. A concern is referred, but nobody knows whether they reached the service. Marks are recorded module by module, while the pattern across them goes unnoticed. One part of the university knows about caring responsibilities; another sees only absence. Nothing necessarily fails. The failure sits in the joins — and those are rarely what institutions measure.

Each part of the institution may have done what it was required to do. The record contains multiple fragments of truth, carefully documented and separately owned. The student lives them all at once. That mismatch will be familiar to anyone who has ever sat with a student while several perfectly reasonable institutional answers fail to add up. But for those fragments to become a coherent experience, someone has to connect them.

Course leaders, personal tutors, module teams, administrators and support staff notice when several small things form a pattern. They translate formal language, recognise when an apparently straightforward case is not quite straightforward, contact another team rather than simply redirecting the student, remember context that is not visible in the current system, and follow up after the formal handover.

This kind of work has a substantial intellectual lineage. Strauss described the ‘articulation work’ required to coordinate complex activity, while Star and Strauss (1999) examined how work essential to keeping systems functioning can remain invisible to formal accounts of what work is. More recent higher education research has similarly drawn attention to boundary-crossing work and the expertise required to operate across institutional divisions (Vere, Verney and Webster-Deakin, 2024).

Pugh (2024) uses the term connective labour for the relational work through which people recognise, read and respond to one another in professions such as teaching and care. The work I am interested in here operates at a different level. It is the interpretive and relational work of connecting the fragments of an institution so that students experience something more coherent than a series of separate systems, teams and processes. I call this institutional connective labour: recognising which elements belong together, what context matters, where apparently routine cases require another look, and when completing a process has not resolved the problem that prompted it.

The work that disappears when it succeeds

Institutional connective labour is remarkably difficult for organisations to see, particularly in the large and distributed environments of higher education. Successful repair tends to leave little trace. An experienced member of staff spots a problem before it escalates, finds the colleague who knows how to resolve it, explains an opaque process, reconciles contradictory information or prevents an administrative delay from affecting progression. Eventually, the student continues. On paper, very little happened. Indeed, the successful outcome can make the system itself appear to have worked. This creates an uncomfortable organisational paradox. The people who are best at compensating for fragmented systems may inadvertently make that fragmentation less visible. Their judgement, memory, relationships and persistence absorb the gaps.

Workload models record formal roles more readily than the accumulation of noticing, translating, connecting and following through around them. Restructures may identify apparent duplication without asking whether overlapping roles are providing connection or resilience. Processes can be streamlined without recognising the informal knowledge through which they were previously made workable.

The visible machinery remains. The less visible capacity that made it function is weakened. As universities become more distributed across campuses, partners, professional services, digital environments and different forms of provision, fragmentation is not necessarily evidence of poor organisation. Complex institutions will always distribute responsibility. But distribution creates a corresponding need for integration. We tend to design carefully for the former and assume the latter will happen.

Greater resolution is not greater understanding

Data and process offer partial institutional views. An attendance pattern can signal a problem without explaining it. A referral records movement through a system without showing whether useful support was reached. A completed process can demonstrate compliance while the original difficulty remains unresolved.

Learning analytics scholars have long warned against treating data as neutral representations of student experience. Signals require interpretation, context and attention to student agency (Slade and Prinsloo, 2013). The same problem extends beyond analytics. Rules, records and processes are representations of reality, not reality itself. Their application still requires decisions about relevance, context and meaning. Informal systems can reproduce inequality, make support dependent on encountering the right person and leave both students and staff unprotected. But neither can the need for context and interpretation simply be designed out.

The difficulty becomes clearest when several individually reasonable accounts do not quite align. Low attendance may indicate disengagement, but it may mean something else entirely. A missed deadline may be habitual delay or the point at which an otherwise successful student can no longer absorb a series of pressures. A student may appear to have been referred successfully while moving repeatedly between services without ever finding somewhere their problem fits. Greater resolution does not necessarily produce greater understanding. Sometimes it simply gives us a more detailed picture of the fragments. The difficulty is not that any one account is false. It is that each tells the truth from only one angle.

Seeing slant

Dickinson’s ‘slant’ offers a useful way of thinking about this. Seeing slant is not an argument for indecision, endless consultation or gathering every possible perspective before acting. It is the recognition that complex experience rarely arrives from one direction. For universities, two questions can help expose the joins:

What alternative stories could produce the pattern we can see?

Where are staff repeatedly having to translate, reconnect or repair what a formal process has separated?

These are questions about judgement rather than additional process. The aim is not to collect every possible view before acting. Universities must simplify, classify and make decisions. But credible judgement requires some awareness of what has been simplified in doing so. The more useful institutional question may therefore be not simply whether a process has been completed, but what had to happen around that process to make it work.

The institution between the boxes

The point is not simply that this work should be recognised. It should tell us something. If staff repeatedly have to reconnect the same processes, translate the same information or recover context lost at the same handover, those interventions are evidence. They show where the formal account of how the institution works diverges from how it works in practice.

That makes institutional connective labour potentially diagnostic. A workaround may solve an immediate problem, but repeated workarounds reveal something more useful: where information stops travelling, where responsibilities do not quite meet, or where a process produces completion without resolution. That does not mean turning connective labour into another metric. Formalising it too heavily would risk flattening the very context and interpretation that make it useful. The point is to create ways for recurring patterns noticed through this work to inform institutional learning without reducing them to another dashboard. Nor should institutions depend on a few experienced individuals to hold the system together. The challenge is to make the conditions for noticing, connecting and escalating less accidental — and the knowledge generated through that work less private.

A practical starting point is to ask, in course reviews, service reviews or handover discussions: where are staff repeatedly having to reconnect what the formal process separates? Then take one recently ‘resolved’ case and ask a simpler question: what had to happen outside the formal process for this to reach a workable outcome? If the same kinds of repair appear repeatedly, that is not merely evidence of helpful staff. It is evidence about where the institution itself needs attention. For the student, the difference between a fragmented institution and a coherent one may simply be whether somebody noticed the joins.

Joanne Irving-Walton is a Principal Lecturer at Teesside University, working across learning and teaching and international partnerships. She is particularly interested in how academic judgement and professional identity develop through the emotional realities of higher education.

title: Chemie-Nobelpreis 2026: Wie aus einem Hauch Asymmetrie Homochiralität entsteht
summary: Wie aus spiegelbildlichen Molekülen eine dominante Form wird: Wir erklären die chemische Selbstverstärkung und was sie über die Einseitigkeit des Lebens aussagt
full_text:
Inhaltsverzeichnis

This article is also available in English. It was translated with technical assistance and editorially reviewed before publication.

.

Der Nobelpreis für Chemie geht in diesem Jahr an den Franzosen Henri B. Kagan und den Japaner Kenso Soai für die Entdeckung nichtlinearer Effekte und der Autokatalyse in der asymmetrischen organischen Synthese. Hinter dieser Formulierung steckt eine Ideenkette, die bis zu Louis Pasteur zurückreicht und ein über ein Jahrhundert altes Rätsel der Chemie löst: Wie kann aus einem Gemisch zweier spiegelbildlicher Moleküle ein Zustand entstehen, in dem nur noch eine Form existiert?

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Spiegelbilder, die das Leben schwer machen

Viele Moleküle kommen in zwei Varianten vor, die sich zueinander verhalten wie rechte und linke Hand – sie sind Spiegelbilder, lassen sich aber nicht zur Deckung bringen. Chemiker nennen solche Moleküle chiral (von griechisch „Hand“). Die beiden Spiegelbildformen heißen Enantiomere. Eine Mischung, die beide Formen zu gleichen Anteilen enthält, nennt man Racemat.

Das Leben hat sich jedoch für eine Seite entschieden: In lebenden Organismen kommen in Proteinen nur L-Aminosäuren und in DNA und RNA nur D-Zucker vor. Dieses Phänomen heißt Homochiralität. Ohne äußeren chiralen Einfluss führt die Synthese von Aminosäuren jedoch stets zum Racemat.

Für die Pharmaindustrie ist die Frage auch praktisch relevant. So zeigte der Thalidomid-Skandal der frühen 1960er-Jahre, wie entscheidend die Enantiomerenreinheit ist: Thalidomid (in Deutschland als Contergan vertrieben) war ein Beruhigungsmittel, das schwangeren Frauen gegen Übelkeit verschrieben wurde. Es stellte sich jedoch heraus, dass das eine Spiegelbild des Wirkstoffs die gewünschte beruhigende Wirkung hatte, während das andere bei Tausenden von Kindern schwere Fehlbildungen verursachte. Allerdings wandeln sich die beiden Formen im Körper binnen kurzer Zeit ineinander um, so dass selbst ein enantiomerenreines Präparat das Unglück nicht sicher verhindert hätte. Der Enantiomerenüberschuss (abgekürzt ee), also der prozentuale Überschuss des einen Enantiomers gegenüber dem anderen, muss daher streng kontrolliert werden.

Von Pasteur zu Frank

Die Ideenkette beginnt bei Louis Pasteur, der an Weinsäurekristallen zwei spiegelbildliche Varianten unterschied und 1857 beobachtete, dass Bakterien nur eines der beiden Weinsäure-Enantiomere verstoffwechseln – das andere blieb unangetastet. Damit zeigte er, dass die Chemie des Lebens chirale Präferenzen hat.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Im frühen 20. Jahrhundert gelang dem deutschen Chemiker Willy Marckwald die erste asymmetrische Reaktion: Er decarboxylierte Methylethylmalonsäure als Salz der chiralen Base Brucin, was die Bildung eines Enantiomers begünstigte. Der Effekt war jedoch bescheiden.

Entscheidend wurde 1953 ein mathematisches Modell des britischen theoretischen Physikers Charles Frank. Damit aus einer minimalen Asymmetrie vollständige Homochiralität entstehen kann, müssen drei Bedingungen erfüllt sein:

Autokatalyse: Das Produkt der Reaktion katalysiert seine eigene Bildung, es beschleunigt also seine eigene Entstehung.

Enantioselektive Katalyse: Die Reaktion bevorzugt ein Enantiomer gegenüber dem anderen.

Gegenseitige Hemmung („mutual antagonism“): Das Produkt wirkt gleichzeitig als Antikatalysator, hemmt also die Bildung seines eigenen Spiegelbilds.

Frank selbst notierte, ein „Nachweis im Labor ist vielleicht nicht unmöglich“. Autokatalyse und enantioselektive Katalyse waren bereits bekannt. Doch ein Reaktionssystem, das beide mit einer gegenseitigen Hemmung der Enantiomere verband und dadurch einen anfänglichen Überschuss einer Händigkeit verstärkte, war bis dahin nicht experimentell nachgewiesen worden.

Kagan: Nichtlineare Effekte

Bis 1986 galt in der Chemie als gesichert, dass der Enantiomerenüberschuss des Produkts (ee des Produkts) linear mit dem Enantiomerenüberschuss des verwendeten chiralen Liganden (einem Molekül, das an das Metall des Katalysators bindet und die Reaktion steuert) korreliert. Verdoppelt man die Reinheit des Liganden, verdoppelt sich auch die Reinheit des Produkts.

Henri Kagan erkannte, dass diese Linearität nur dann gilt, wenn am Katalysator genau ein Ligand beteiligt ist. Katalysatoren bestehen oft aus einem Metallatom (M) mit einem oder mehreren Liganden (L*). Kagan nahm an, dass das Metall mindestens zwei Liganden gleichzeitig bindet (ein sogenannter ML*2-Komplex). Wenn der Ligand nicht enantiomerenrein ist, können sich drei verschiedene Katalysatorformen bilden: zwei homochirale Komplexe (beide Liganden haben dieselbe Händigkeit: rechts-rechts oder links-links) und ein heterochiraler Komplex (ein Rechts- und ein Links-Ligand).

Der heterochirale Komplex und die homochiralen Komplexe verhalten sich zueinander wie Diastereomere – das heißt Moleküle, die zwar dieselben Bausteine enthalten, aber räumlich unterschiedlich angeordnet sind und sich nicht wie Bild und Spiegelbild verhalten. Diastereomere haben unterschiedliche physikalische und chemische Eigenschaften, also auch unterschiedliche Reaktionsgeschwindigkeiten.

Ist der heterochirale Komplex weniger reaktiv als die homochiralen, dann entsteht ein positiver nichtlinearer Effekt (+NLE): Das Produkt ist enantiomerenreiner, als man es vom Liganden erwarten würde. Ist der heterochirale Komplex reaktiver, entsteht ein negativer NLE (−NLE), und das Produkt ist weniger enantiomerenrein als erwartet. Kagan führte dafür einen Korrekturfaktor f ein, der das Verhältnis von heterochiralem zu homochiralem Katalysator und deren relative Reaktivität berücksichtigt.

Kagan konnte dies 1986 an drei Reaktionen demonstrieren, darunter die Sharpless-Epoxidierung von Geraniol (eine Reaktion, bei der ein Alken zu einem Epoxid – einem dreigliedrigen Ring mit Sauerstoff – umgesetzt wird), die einen positiven NLE zeigte. Ein weiteres Beispiel ist das System von Ryoji Noyori. Bei der Addition von Diethylzink an Benzaldehyd mit dem Liganden (−)-DAIB lieferte ein Liganden-ee von nur 15 Prozent ein Produkt mit einem ee von 95 Prozent. Der Grund ist ein Reservoir-Effekt: Der heterochirale Komplex ist thermodynamisch stabiler und entzieht das Minderenantiomer des Liganden der Katalyse.

Soai: Autokatalyse mit Verstärkung

Kenso Soai untersuchte die Addition von Diisopropylzink an Pyridin-3-carbaldehyd. Das Produkt – ein Alkohol – wirkt dabei als eigener Katalysator (Autokatalyse genannt). 1990 zeigte er dies erstmals, allerdings mit Verlust an Enantiomerenreinheit: Das Produkt hatte nur 35 Prozent ee, der eingesetzte Katalysator 86 Prozent.

Fünf Jahre später gelang der Durchbruch mit Pyrimidin-5-carbaldehyd als Substrat: Ausgehend von nur 2 Prozent ee stieg der Enantiomerenüberschuss über vier aufeinanderfolgende Reaktionszyklen auf 88 Prozent. Die Reaktion verstärkte den Überschuss des anfangs häufigeren Enantiomers. Damit waren alle drei Bedingungen des Frank-Modells erfüllt.

Besonders spektakulär ist ein alkinylsubstituiertes Derivat: Dort führte ein Start-ee von 0,00005 Prozent nach drei Durchgängen zu über 99,5 Prozent ee. Der Enantiomerenüberschuss gibt die prozentuale Differenz zwischen den beiden Formen an. Die Stoffmenge des anfangs minimal überwiegenden Enantiomers wuchs dabei um den Faktor 630.000, die des anderen um weniger als das Tausendfache. Aus einem nahezu exakten 1:1-Gemisch wurde so ein Zustand, in dem ein Enantiomer das andere um fast das 400-Fache überwog.

Symmetriebrechung aus dem Nichts

Noch verblüffender ist die absolute asymmetrische Synthese: Hier startet die Reaktion ohne jeglichen chiralen Einfluss. Das Zinkalkoxid (eine Zink-Sauerstoff-Verbindung, die als Zwischenprodukt entsteht) bildet sich zunächst als Racemat. Aufgrund statistischer Schwankungen – der Stereochemiker Kurt Mislow sprach von Kryptochiralität, einer mit üblichen Methoden nicht messbaren Chiralität – entsteht jedoch ein winziger Überschuss eines Enantiomers, den die Soai-Reaktion dann massiv verstärkt.

In 37 Experimenten ergaben 18 das (R)-Produkt und 19 das (S)-Produkt, mit ee-Werten von 15 bis 91 Prozent. Welches Enantiomer „gewinnt“, ist also reiner Zufall – aber die Reaktion bricht die Symmetrie und führt zu fast vollständiger Homochiralität.

Mechanismus noch nicht abschließend geklärt

Die Aufklärung des Reaktionsmechanismus beschäftigt die chemische Community seit Jahrzehnten. Zunächst deuteten kinetische Daten auf einen dimeren (aus zwei Einheiten aufgebauten) Katalysator hin, später auf einen tetrameren (aus vier Einheiten aufgebauten). DFT-Rechnungen (Dichtefunktionaltheorie, ein quantenchemisches Berechnungsverfahren) führten zu einem sogenannten Square-Macrocycle-Square-Modell (SMS): zwei quadratische Zink-Sauerstoff-Dimere, die über einen zwölfgliedrigen Makrocyclus verbunden sind. 2015 gelang Matsumoto, Kawasaki und Soai die Kristallstrukturanalyse homo- und heterochiraler Tetramere, deren Verknüpfung diesem Modell ähnelt. Heute stehen zwei detaillierte Modelle nebeneinander:

Denmark et al.: Das Substrat bindet „Floor-to-floor“ (ebenenweise) an das homochirale Tetramer über zwei koordinativ ungesättigte Zinkatome. Beim heterochiralen Tetramer ist diese Anordnung geometrisch benachteiligt. Das erklärt, warum das homochirale Tetramer die Reaktion bevorzugt.

Trapp et al.: Zinkhalbacetal-Komplexe (Verbindungen aus Zink, Sauerstoff und Kohlenstoff) sind entscheidend; die Verstärkung beruht auf einem kinetisch kontrollierten Nichtgleichgewichtszustand. Dieser Ansatz unterscheidet sich vom Mechanismus nach Kagan und Frank.

Beide Modelle könnten nebeneinander gelten, da sie mit unterschiedlichen Substraten erarbeitet wurden.

Allerdings bleibt die Soai-Reaktion ein künstliches Laborexperiment. Sie beweist zwar, dass das theoretische Modell von Charles Frank in der Praxis funktioniert und sich Chiralität also spontan verstärken lässt. Allerdings läuft die Reaktion mit speziellen Zinkverbindungen ab und funktioniert nicht in Wasser. Da das Leben aber in einer wässrigen Umgebung entstanden ist, war die Soai-Reaktion höchstwahrscheinlich nicht der Auslöser für die biologische Homochiralität vor 3,5 bis 4 Milliarden Jahren. Die Forscher haben damit also gezeigt, dass der Mechanismus der Selbstverstärkung grundsätzlich möglich ist. Die Suche nach dem exakten chemischen Weg, der das Leben einseitig gemacht hat, geht jedoch weiter.
